note: Dates are rounded figures from the geological and palaeontological literature, entered from memory and not yet tied to citations. They are context for the reader and are not produced by the plate model.

stages.title: Part of Gondwana
stages.text: The Indian landmass lies in the southern hemisphere, joined to Africa, Madagascar, Antarctica and Australia.

stages.title: Gondwana breaks apart
stages.text: Rifting separates East Gondwana (India, Madagascar, Antarctica, Australia) from Africa, and then India–Madagascar from Antarctica–Australia.

stages.title: Adrift with Madagascar
stages.text: India and Madagascar move together until they separate, usually dated to about 90–85 million years ago.

stages.title: The fast run north
stages.text: India crosses the ocean unusually quickly. Near 66 million years ago the Deccan Traps erupt across its western side.

stages.title: Meeting Asia
stages.text: The first contact with Asia is usually placed at about 55–50 million years ago; estimates range from roughly 59 to 34. Northward motion slows sharply.

stages.title: Raising the Himalaya
stages.text: Continued convergence thickens the crust and lifts the Himalaya and Tibet. India is still moving north by a few centimetres a year.

events.title: End-Triassic mass extinction
events.text: A large share of marine and land species disappears; dinosaurs become the dominant land animals afterwards.

events.title: Karoo–Ferrar eruptions
events.text: Vast lava outpourings across southern Gondwana, linked to its first rifting.

events.title: Late Jurassic
events.text: Giant sauropods; the earliest known birds appear in the fossil record.

events.title: Flowering plants spread
events.text: Angiosperms diversify through the Early Cretaceous.

events.title: Mid-Cretaceous hothouse
events.text: High sea levels flood continental interiors; no polar ice caps.

events.title: Chicxulub impact and Deccan Traps
events.text: An asteroid strikes what is now Mexico while the Deccan lavas erupt across western India. Non-avian dinosaurs die out.

events.title: Palaeocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
events.text: A sharp global warming episode lasting on the order of a hundred thousand years.

events.title: Early whales
events.text: The earliest whales are found in rocks of this age in what is now Pakistan and India.

events.title: Antarctica freezes
events.text: Permanent ice sheets begin to form as the climate cools.

events.title: Grasslands expand
events.text: Open grassland ecosystems spread through the Miocene.

events.title: Himalaya and monsoon
events.text: A high Himalaya and Tibetan plateau are in place; the South Asian monsoon strengthens over the Miocene.

events.title: Human and chimpanzee lineages diverge
events.text: Usually placed between about 7 and 6 million years ago, in Africa.

events.title: Ice ages begin
events.text: Northern hemisphere glaciation sets in from about 2.6 million years ago; early stone tools appear in Africa.

events.title: Humans
events.text: Homo sapiens appears about 300,000 years ago. All of recorded history fits inside the last step of this timeline.
